title: SPHEREx near-infrared images show that the September 2025 ASASSN-14ko flare peaked 21 days after the Payne et al. 2022 ephemeris; the August 2026 flare peak time depends on its decline time
abstract: Question: do the 2025-2026 flares of the repeating nuclear transient ASASSN-14ko arrive at the times of the Payne et al. (2022) constant-Pdot ephemeris? No public optical or UV survey covers the 2026 flares. Approach: we used 541 public SPHEREx Level-2 spectral images (0.75-5 um; QR2 and QR3) from three windows: 2025 Aug-Oct, 2026 Feb-Apr and 2026 Aug-Oct. We did forced aperture photometry of the nucleus, calibrated the windows with three field stars, and fitted a host spectrum plus flare profiles (0.75-2.4 um) on a grid of peak times. Results: the flares are detected (chi2 improvement 100.9). Flare n = 37 peaked at MJD 60936 (2-sigma 60931-60939), +20.6 d after the Payne et al. forecast. At the forecast peak the 1.1-1.6 um excess was -0.12 +/- 0.07 mJy; the excess appeared after MJD 60928. The forecast time gives delta chi2 = 11.6 (8.3-15.5 in 21 variants; 3.5-5.1 with less 1.6-2.4 um information). This offset equals the +20.5 d offset of the TESS flare n = 38, and the n = 37 to n = 38 interval is 104.4 d. Flare n = 40 (2026 August) is present only in decline. Its peak is not later than MJD 61267. The Payne et al. time is excluded for a 14.86-d decline (delta chi2 = 32.5) but allowed for a decline time of 20-30 d, which the data do not constrain. The QR3 photometric scale is 3.7 +/- 0.5 percent lower than QR2 at 0.75-1.1 um for field stars; without this correction most of the n = 40 excess disappears. The 2.4-3.8 um flux of the nucleus rose by 4.2 percent from 2025 to early 2026. Updated forecasts: n = 41 near 2026-11-24 (constant P = 108.09 d, +/- 4.7 d), against 2026-10-18 from Payne et al. Limitations: one 50-day window per flare, host spectrum from window comparison, the optical flare shape is assumed, and n = 40 timing depends on calibration and decline time.

display.caption: SPHEREx flux excess of the ASASSN-14ko nucleus over the host model, scaled to 0.9 um, in the three observing windows. Green: best fit. Red dashed: flares at the Payne et al. (2022) times with the n = 37 amplitude. Dotted lines: forecast peak times.
Profiled delta chi2 for the peak time of flare n = 37 (left) and flare n = 40 (right, for four decline times, amplitude A40 <= 3 A37). Dashed lines: forecasts.

Observed minus calculated peak times relative to the Payne et al. (2022) ephemeris. Grey: published peaks. Dark: ASAS-SN and TESS (SCI 9398601f). Orange: SPHEREx n = 37 and the n = 40 range for decline times of 10-30 d.

citations.reason: We use its peak times, flare profile and forecasts. Our SPHEREx n = 37 time agrees with its late-arrival result and its TESS n = 38 offset.
The n = 37 to n = 38 interval of 104.4 d agrees with its random period changes of order 0.6 d per orbit or larger.
We test its 2026 forecast and confirm the late arrival with a fourth instrument.
Related forecast test of a repeating partial disruption (AT2018fyk). It notes the lack of Swift coverage in 2026.
Our near-infrared marker is independent of the UV-to-optical marker relation that this work questions.
Variable emission delays can also explain the late times; we do not separate this.
Our new interval supports period noise beyond a smooth trend.
Its constant-Pdot ephemeris predicts the n = 37 peak 20.6 d too early.
